nodes.name: Continuous MPUM (informal)
nodes.statement:
A model satisfying all 
conditions is abbreviatory called continuous $\mathrm{MPUM}$ 
(most powerful unfalsified model).

nodes.name: Field K and operator algebra O
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a field and $O$ be an operator algebra over $K$.

nodes.name: Function space A_O
nodes.statement:
Further 
let $\mathcal{A}_O$ be a function space over $K$ possessing an $O$-module structure.

nodes.name: Behavior (model)
nodes.statement:
A \textbf{model} or a so-called \textbf{behavior} $\mathcal{B}$ is the solution
set 
of a homogeneous linear system, given by finitely many equations. These equations are defined in terms of
the operator algebra $O$.
nodes.statement_short: A behavior is the solution set of a finite homogeneous linear system of operator equations over $O$.

nodes.name: Solution set Sol and module action bullet
nodes.statement:
Thus $\mathcal{B}$ is characterized by
$$ \mathcal{B}=\mathrm{Sol}(O^{1\times r}R)= \lbrace \omega \in \mathcal{A}_O^m \, | \, R \bullet \omega= 0 \rbrace, \;\;\; 
\mbox{ where } \; R\in O^{r \times m}$$
and $\bullet$ denotes the natural extension of the module action $o \bullet \omega$ of 
$o \in O$ on $\omega \in \mathcal{A}_O$ to the matrix $R \in O^{r \times m}$ and the vector
$\omega \in \mathcal{A}_O^m$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{B}=\mathrm{Sol}(O^{1\times r}R)$ = solutions of $R\bullet\omega=0$; $\bullet$ extends the module action to matrices.

nodes.name: Observed signal set Omega
nodes.statement:
Suppose we observe a set of signals 
$\Omega \subseteq \mathcal{A}_O^m$.

nodes.name: Linear exact modeling problem
nodes.statement_short: Find a behavior $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ in the model class containing $\Omega$ and contained in every behavior that contains $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Most powerful unfalsified model (MPUM)
nodes.statement:
If $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ is invariant under the action of $O$, that is,
if we have for all $o \in O$ 
$$ \omega \in \mathcal{B} \;\; \Rightarrow  \;\; o \bullet \omega \in \mathcal{B},$$ 
it is called \textbf{most powerful unfalsified model}, 
short $\mathrm{MPUM}$ of $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Variant most powerful unfalsified model (VMPUM)
nodes.statement:
Else, if $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ varies under $O$ it is called 
\textbf{variant most powerful unfalsified model}, short $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Notation B_Omega^V
nodes.statement: We denote the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $\Omega$ by $\mathcal{B}_\Omega^V$.

nodes.name: Motivating example: MPUM vs VMPUM of omega(t)=t
nodes.statement:
Consider the signal set consisting of a single signal 
$$\Omega= \lbrace \omega \rbrace, \;\;\; \mbox{where } \; \omega(t)=t \;  \mbox{ for all  } t \in \mathbb{R} .$$ 
\begin{enumerate}
\item Let $O=\mathbb{C}[\partial]$ and $\mathcal{A}_O=\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C})$, where 
$\partial \bullet f := \frac{df}{dt}$. Using the commutative structure of the operator ring, the underlying system is invariant under 
differentiation:
$$ R \bullet w = 0 \;\;\; \Rightarrow \;\;\; R ( \partial \bullet w ) = 
( R \partial ) \bullet w =  ( \partial R ) \bullet w
=   \partial ( R \bullet w) =0.$$
Since we are searching for a differentiation-invariant model, we obtain that besides $\omega$, also 
its derivative, the constant function $1$, belongs to $\mathcal{B}_{\Omega} $. Using that the model is $\mathbb{C}$-linear, we get that
$$\mathcal{B}_{\Omega} = \{ w  \ | \ \exists a,b \in \mathbb{C}: \forall t\in \mathbb{R} : w(t)=at+b \}.$$
An element $w \in  \mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C})$ is contained in $\mathcal{B}_\Omega$ if and only if
$$\partial^2 \bullet w=0,$$
i.e. the $\mathrm{MPUM}$ is specified by a single ordinary differential equation with constant coefficients.
\item Now let $O=\mathbb{C}[t]\langle \partial \rangle$, where 
$\partial \bullet f := \frac{df}{dt}$ and $\mathcal{A}_O$ is defined as above. We want to describe 
$\omega$ as a solution of homogeneous ordinary differential equations with polynomial coefficients. The 
equations $$\partial^2 \bullet w=0 \;\; \mbox{ and } \;\; t \partial \bullet  w-w=0 $$
are satisfied by $\omega$. We will see later that these two generate a kernel representation of the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $\Omega$.
The corresponding solution space equals $$\mathcal{B}_\Omega^V=\{ w \ | \ \exists a \in \mathbb{C} : \forall t\in{\mathbb{R}} : w(t)=at\}.$$
Notice that this example demonstrates the variance under $\partial$, since we have
$ \partial \bullet \omega \notin \mathcal{B}_\Omega^V$.
Another property that should be pointed out is that the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ yields a more
precise description of $\Omega$ than $\mathrm{MPUM}$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For $\omega(t)=t$: the MPUM over $\mathbb{C}[\partial]$ is $\{at+b\}$, while the VMPUM over $\mathbb{C}[t]\langle\partial\rangle$ is $\{at\}$.
nodes.label: MotivatingExample

nodes.name: Skew polynomial ring / Ore extension / Ore algebra
nodes.statement:
\cite{MR} \ \begin{enumerate} 
\item[(1)] Let $A$ be a ring and $\sigma : A \rightarrow A$ be a ring endomorphism.
\begin{enumerate} 
\item The map $\delta : A \rightarrow A$ is called a $\sigma$-\textbf{derivation} if it is 
$K$-linear and satisfies the skew Leibniz rule
\begin{align} \delta(a b) = \sigma(a) \delta(b) + \delta(a) b \;\;\;\; \mbox{for all } a, b \in A.
\end{align}
\item For a $\sigma$-derivation $\delta$, the ring $A\left[ \partial;\sigma, \delta \right] $ 
which
consists of all polynomials in $\partial$ with coefficients in $A$ with the usual addition 
and a product defined by the commutation rule
$$\partial a = \sigma(a) \partial + \delta(a) \;\;\;\; \mbox{for all } a \in A,$$
is called a \textbf{skew polynomial ring} or an \textbf{Ore extension} of $A$ with $\sigma$ and $\delta$.
\end{enumerate}
\item[] If $A$ is a domain and $\sigma$ is injective, the 
skew polynomial ring $A\left[ \partial;\sigma, \delta \right]$ is a domain by degree arguments. 
Then the definition can be iterated to the so-called Ore algebras \cite{CS}.
\item[(2)] Let $A=K[t_1, \dots, t_n]$. An iterated skew polynomial ring 
$$O=K[t_1, \dots, t_n] [\partial_1;\sigma_1, \delta_1]  \cdots [\partial_s;\sigma_s, \delta_s]$$ 
is called a (polynomial) \textbf{Ore algebra} if the $\sigma_i$'s and $\delta_j$'s commute for $ 1 \leq i , j \leq s $, 
the $\partial_i$'s commute with $\partial_j$'s and further for all $1\leq i \leq s$ the map $\sigma_i:O \rightarrow O$ is 
an injective $K$-algebra endomorphism and $\delta_i:O \rightarrow O $ is a $\sigma_i$-derivation satisfying
$ \sigma_i( \partial_j)= \partial_j \;\;\;\; \mbox{ and }\;\;\;\; \delta_i(\partial_j)=0. $
\end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Defines $\sigma$-derivations, Ore extensions $A[\partial;\sigma,\delta]$ with $\partial a=\sigma(a)\partial+\delta(a)$, and iterated polynomial Ore algebras.
nodes.label: defOre

nodes.name: Skew Leibniz rule
nodes.statement: \delta(a b) = \sigma(a) \delta(b) + \delta(a) b \;\;\;\; \mbox{for all } a, b \in A.
nodes.label: deltaOperation

nodes.name: Normal form in an Ore algebra
nodes.statement:
Using multi-index notation, every element of an Ore algebra can be expressed into the normal form
$$
\sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0^s} p_\alpha \partial^\alpha  = 
\sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0^s} p_\alpha {\partial_1}^{\alpha_1} \cdot \ldots \cdot {\partial_s}^{\alpha_s}  
\;\;\;\; \mbox{ where } \;\; p_\alpha \in A.
$$
conclusions: every element of an Ore algebra can be expressed into the normal form

nodes.name: Weyl, difference, SW and q-difference algebras
nodes.statement:
Let $n=1$, thus $A=K[t]$. The algebras can be iterated to $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The first \textbf{Weyl algebra} is defined by

$\mathrm{W}_1:= A[ \partial; \mathrm{id}_{ \mathrm{W}_1}, \frac{\partial}{\partial t}]$

with the commutation rule $ \partial  t = t \partial + 1 .$
\item The first \textbf{difference algebra} is defined by
$ \mathcal{S}_1 :=A \left[ \Delta; \sigma, \delta \right]$,
where $ (\sigma p)(t) =  p(t + 1)$ and $\delta(p)=\sigma(p)-p$ for all 
$p \in \mathcal{S}_1$. The commutation rule is
$ \Delta t = t \Delta + \Delta + 1.$
\item The following Ore algebra is a combination of the first and second one. Define
$\mathcal{SW}_1:=A \left[ \Delta; \sigma_1, \delta_1 \right]\left[ \partial; \sigma_2, \delta_2 \right]$,
where $\sigma_2:=id_{ \mathcal{SW}_1 }$, $\delta_2:=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}$ and $ (\sigma_1 p)(t) = p(t + 1)$, 
$\delta_1(p)=\sigma_1(p)-p$ for all $p \in \mathcal{SW}_1$. Then $ \partial t = t \partial + 1$,
$\Delta t = t \Delta + \Delta +1$ and $\partial \Delta = \Delta \partial$.
\item Suppose $q$ to be a parameter. The first \textbf{continuous $q$-difference algebra} is defined by
$ \mathcal{Q}:= A [\partial; \sigma, \delta], $
where $\sigma( p )=p(q t)$ and $\delta(p)= p(qt)-p(t)$. We obtain the commutation rule
$ \partial t = qt \partial + (q-1)t$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Defines the first Weyl algebra, difference algebra, their combination $\mathcal{SW}_1$ and the continuous $q$-difference algebra with their commutation rules.
nodes.label: interestingAlgebras

nodes.name: Ore extension shift isomorphism
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be a ring, and $A[\partial; \sigma,\delta]$ be an Ore extension of $A$. 
For any $\alpha \in A$ there exists an Ore extension $A[\Delta_{\alpha}; \sigma,\delta']$
with $\delta'(a) = \sigma(a) \alpha - \alpha a + \delta(a)$, such that 
$A[\partial; \sigma,\delta] \cong A[\Delta_{\alpha}; \sigma,\delta'] $ as rings.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a ring, and $A[\partial; \sigma,\delta]$ be an Ore extension of $A$.
conclusions:
there exists an Ore extension $A[\Delta_{\alpha}; \sigma,\delta']$
with $\delta'(a) = \sigma(a) \alpha - \alpha a + \delta(a)$, such that 
$A[\partial; \sigma,\delta] \cong A[\Delta_{\alpha}; \sigma,\delta'] $ as rings.
nodes.statement_short: Replacing $\partial$ by $\partial-\alpha$ gives an isomorphic Ore extension with modified derivation $\delta'$.
nodes.label: OreIso

nodes.name: A is an O-module
nodes.statement:
Let 
$O:=

A[\partial_1; \sigma_1,\delta_1]\cdots[\partial_m; \sigma_m,\delta_m]$ be an Ore algebra.
 With the action
$$
\partial_i \bullet p := \delta_i(p)  \;\;\; \mbox{ and } \;\;\; a \bullet p :=a \cdot p \;\;\; \mbox{ for all } p\in A \mbox{ and } a \in A
$$
the $K$-algebra $A$ becomes an $O$-module.
conclusions: the $K$-algebra $A$ becomes an $O$-module
nodes.statement_short: With $\partial_i\bullet p=\delta_i(p)$ and multiplication by $A$, $A$ becomes an $O$-module.

nodes.name: Proof that A is an O-module
nodes.statement:
For this, we have to show that 
\begin{enumerate}
 \item $ (o_1 \cdot o_2) \bullet p = o_1 \bullet ( o_2 \bullet p ) \;\;\;\; $ for all $o_1, o_2 \in O$ and $p \in A$ 
 \item $ (o_1 + o_2) \bullet p = o_1 \bullet p +  o_2 \bullet p \;\;\;\; $ for all $o_1, o_2 \in O$ and $p \in A$ 
 \item $ o \bullet (p+q) = o \bullet p + o \bullet q \;\;\;\; $ for all $o \in O$ and $p, q \in A.$ 
\end{enumerate}
To show 1. it suffices to consider $o_1=a \partial_i$ and $o_2= b \partial_j$ with $a, b \in A$. Then
\begin{eqnarray*}
 (o_1 \cdot o_2) \bullet p & = & (\, a( \, \sigma_i(b) \partial_i + \delta_i(b)\,) \partial_j \,) \bullet p 
 =  (\, a\sigma_i(b) \partial_i \partial_j + a\delta_i(b) \partial_j \,) \bullet p \\
& = & a\sigma_i(b) \delta_i(p) \delta_j(p) + a\delta_i(b) \delta_j(p)
 =  a \, \delta_i (b\delta_j(p))
 =  a \partial_i \bullet (\, b \partial_j \bullet p \,)\\
& = &  o_1 \bullet (\, o_2 \bullet p \,).
\end{eqnarray*}
The equality in 2. and 3. holds by similar arguments.
nodes.statement_short: Check the module axioms; associativity verified on monomials $a\partial_i$, $b\partial_j$, the rest similarly.

nodes.name: Module axioms to verify
nodes.statement_short: List the three module axioms to check.

nodes.name: Verify associativity
nodes.statement:
To show 1. it suffices to consider $o_1=a \partial_i$ and $o_2= b \partial_j$ with $a, b \in A$. Then
\begin{eqnarray*}
 (o_1 \cdot o_2) \bullet p & = & (\, a( \, \sigma_i(b) \partial_i + \delta_i(b)\,) \partial_j \,) \bullet p 
 =  (\, a\sigma_i(b) \partial_i \partial_j + a\delta_i(b) \partial_j \,) \bullet p \\
& = & a\sigma_i(b) \delta_i(p) \delta_j(p) + a\delta_i(b) \delta_j(p)
 =  a \, \delta_i (b\delta_j(p))
 =  a \partial_i \bullet (\, b \partial_j \bullet p \,)\\
& = &  o_1 \bullet (\, o_2 \bullet p \,).
\end{eqnarray*}
The equality in 2. and 3. holds by similar arguments.
nodes.statement_short: Verify axiom 1 on monomials; axioms 2, 3 similarly.

nodes.name: Kernel ker_A f of an operator
nodes.statement: Using this action, we can define the kernel of a linear operator $f$ from the Ore algebra $O$ over a ring $A$ to be $\ker_{A} f := \{ a\in A \mid f \bullet a = 0\}$, which is a $K$-vector space.

nodes.name: Operators with trivial derivation
nodes.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, $A$ be a $K$-algebra, $\partial$ be a $K$-linear operator, acting on $A$ and $B = A[\partial; \sigma, \delta]$ be the corresponding operator algebra (that is, for all $a \in A$ we have $ \partial a = \sigma(a) \partial + \delta(a)$). Then the following holds:

(i) $\ker_A \partial = A \Leftrightarrow \delta = 0 \Leftrightarrow B = A[\partial; \sigma, 0]$.
 

(ii) If $\ker_A \partial = A$, then we have for $\Delta := \partial - 1$:
$A[\partial; \sigma, 0]$ is isomorphic as $K$-algebra to operator algebra $A[\Delta; \sigma, \delta']$ with $\delta' := \sigma - 1$. Moreover, 
$\ker_A \Delta = \{a\in A\mid \sigma(a) = a\} = \mathrm{const}_{\sigma} A \subseteq A$ with the
equality if and only if $A$ is invariant under $\sigma$, what is the case if $\sigma = 1_A$.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a field, $A$ be a $K$-algebra, $\partial$ be a $K$-linear operator, acting on $A$ and $B = A[\partial; \sigma, \delta]$ be the corresponding operator algebra
conclusions: $\ker_A \partial = A \Leftrightarrow \delta = 0 \Leftrightarrow B = A[\partial; \sigma, 0]$
$A[\partial; \sigma, 0]$ is isomorphic as $K$-algebra to operator algebra $A[\Delta; \sigma, \delta']$ with $\delta' := \sigma - 1$
$\ker_A \partial = A \Leftrightarrow \delta = 0 \Leftrightarrow B = A[\partial; \sigma, 0]$
$A[\partial; \sigma, 0]$ is isomorphic as $K$-algebra to operator algebra $A[\Delta; \sigma, \delta']$ with $\delta' := \sigma - 1$

nodes.statement_short: $\partial$ acts trivially iff $\delta=0$; then $\Delta=\partial-1$ gives an isomorphic algebra with $\ker\Delta$ the $\sigma$-constants.
nodes.label: CorDelta

nodes.name: Nontrivial operator
nodes.statement:
Using Lemmata \ref{OreIso} and \ref{CorDelta}, we pass to the new setting of operators, 
which action $\bullet$ is nontrivial on $A$. We call such an operator nontrivial and
from now on, we work with such operators only.

nodes.name: Forward shift algebra and Manin's quantum plane
nodes.statement:
Consider the two most important operator algebras, built from operators having zero kernels.
The first \textbf{forward shift algebra} is defined by
$K[t] \left[ s; \sigma, 0 \right]$ with $(\sigma f)(t) =  f(t + 1)$ for all $f \in K[t]$.
The commutation rule is $s t = t s + s$. There is a natural operator associated to $s$, namely the difference operator $\Delta = s-1$, already defined in \ref{interestingAlgebras}, obeying the relation $\Delta t = t \Delta + \Delta + 1$. Applying Lemma \ref{CorDelta}, we see by degree argument, that $\ker \Delta = K$ and the two algebras are isomorphic both as Ore extensions and $K$-algebras. \\
Let $q$ be transcendental over $K$. Then the first \textbf{$q$-commutative algebra} (or Manin's quantum plane) is defined as $K_q[x,y]:=K(q)[x][\partial;\sigma,0]$ with $(\sigma f)(x)=f(qx)$ for $f\in K[t]$. Again, there is a natural $q$-difference operator $\Delta_q := \partial - 1$ and the corresponding operator algebra has been already described in 
\ref{interestingAlgebras} as the first  continuous $q$-difference algebra. Its commutation rule reads as $\partial t = qt \partial + (q-1)t$.
nodes.statement_short: Forward shift algebra $K[t][s;\sigma,0]$ and $q$-commutative algebra, with their difference operators $\Delta=s-1$, $\Delta_q=\partial-1$.

nodes.name: Left submodule generated notation
nodes.statement: For $o_1, \dots, o_k \in O^{n}$, we denote by ${}_O \langle o_1, \dots o_k \rangle$ the left submodule of $O^n$, generated by $o_1, \dots, o_k$.

nodes.name: O modulo the operator ideal is isomorphic to A
nodes.statement:
Let $O$ be an Ore $A$-algebra, built from operators $\partial_1, \dots, \partial_s$ which have non-zero kernels. Then there is an isomorphism of left $O$-modules 
$$ O/ {}_O \langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle \cong A. $$
assumptions: Let $O$ be an Ore $A$-algebra, built from operators $\partial_1, \dots, \partial_s$ which have non-zero kernels.
conclusions:
there is an isomorphism of left $O$-modules 
$$ O/ {}_O \langle \partial_1, \dots, \partial_s \rangle \cong A. $$
nodes.label: IsoOrePoly

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.7
nodes.statement:
There is a left $O$-module homomorphism 
$$
\varphi : O \rightarrow A, \;\;\; a=\sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0^s} a_{\alpha} \partial^\alpha \mapsto a \bullet 1 
$$

nodes.name: Finiteness of ker kappa_p and Ann_O(p) for tuples
nodes.statement:
If $O$ is Noetherian (see \cite{MR}), then the left submodule 
$\ker(\kappa_p) \subseteq O^{1 \times m}$ is finitely generated. \\

For a polynomial $m$-tuple $p\in A^m$, we consider 
\[
\mathrm{Ann}_O (p) = \{ o\in O \mid o \bullet p = 0 \} = 
\{ o\in O \mid o \bullet p_i = 0 \ \forall \ i \} = 
\bigcap \mathrm{Ann}_O (p_i),
\]
which is a left ideal in $O$. As we see immediately,
$\mathrm{Ann}_O (p)^{1\times m}$ is a (usually strict) submodule
of $\ker(\kappa_p)$ and hence, the latter typically has 

more interesting structure, see Example \ref{exKerP}. It is
always possible to recover $\mathrm{Ann}_O (p)$ from $\ker(\kappa_p)$.
In our opinion, using $\ker(\kappa_p)$ is more natural in the
context of vectors of signals.

Let $\{e_i \}$ be the canonical basis of the free module

nodes.name: Elimination of module components and kernel of a homomorphism
nodes.statement:
\begin{enumerate}

\item \textit{``Elimination of module components''}. \\

Let $S\subset O^{1\times \ell}$ be a submodule. Moreover, let $<_O$ be a monomial ordering on $O$ and $<_m=(c,<_O)$ be a \textit{position over term} monomial module ordering on the free module $O^{1\times \ell}$, defined as follows.  The components are ordered in a descending way $e_1 > \dots > e_{\ell}$ and for any monomials $o_1, o_2 \in O$
\[
o_1 e_i <_m  o_2 e_j \; \Leftrightarrow \; j < i \; \text{ or } \; (j = i 
\text{ and } o_1 <_O o_2).
\]
Let $G$ be a Gr\"obner basis of $S$ with respect to $<_m$. Then $\forall \; 1\leq k < \ell \;\;$ $G \cap \overset{\ell}{\underset{i=k}{\oplus}} O e_i$ is a Gr\"obner basis of $S \cap\overset{\ell}{\underset{i=k}{\oplus}} O e_i$. 


\item \textit{``Kernel of a homomorphism of modules''}. \\

Consider an $O$-module homomorphism $O^{1 \times s} \stackrel{\psi}{\rightarrow} O^{1 \times n}/ O^{1\times m}P $, $e_i \mapsto [\Psi_i]$, where $\Psi_i \in O^{1 \times n}$. Let $P_i$ be the $i$-th row of the matrix $P$. Then
\[
\ker \psi = \mathrm{LeftSyz}( \ (\Psi_1,\ldots,\Psi_s,P_1,\ldots,P_m) \ ) \cap \bigoplus_{i=1}^s O e_i.
\]

\end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Define $W= \overset{\ell}{\underset{i=k}{\bigoplus}} O e_i$. Since $G$ is a Gr\"obner basis of $S$, for any $s \in S$ there exists $g \in G$ such that $\mathrm{lm}(g)$ divides $\mathrm{lm}(s)$. If $s\in S \cap W$, then $\mathrm{lm}(g) \in W$ and hence, by definition of $<_m$, we have $g \in W$ and $g \in G \cap W$. So, $G \cap W$ is a Gr\"obner basis of $S\cap W$.
\item We have \[
[b_1,\ldots,b_s] \in \ker \psi \ \Leftrightarrow \ \exists a_k\in O \ : \ 
\sum_{i=1}^s b_i \Psi_i + \sum_{k=1}^m a_k P_k =0 \ \Leftrightarrow

[b_1,\ldots,b_s] \in \mathrm{LeftSyz}(\ (\Psi_1,\ldots,\Psi_s,P_1,\ldots,P_m)\ ) \cap \bigoplus_{i=1}^s O e_i.
\]

\end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Annihilator in a module and intersection of submodules
nodes.statement:
\begin{enumerate}

\item \textit{``Annihilator of an element in a module''}. \\

Let $M = O^{1 \times n}/O^{1\times m}P$ and let $P_1,\ldots,P_m$ be the 
rows of $P$.
Moreover, let $v \in O^{1\times n}$. Then the left ideal 
$\mathrm{Ann}_M^{O} (v) := \{ a\in O \mid a[v] = 0 \in M\}\subseteq O$ 
can be computed as
\[
\mathrm{Ann}_M^{O} (v) 
= \ker (O \stackrel{\cdot [v]}{\rightarrow} M)
= \mathrm{LeftSyz}(\ (v,P_1,\ldots,P_m)\ ) \cap O e_1.
\]





\item \textit{"Intersection of finitely many submodules''}. \\

Let $N_1, \ldots, N_m \subset O^{1\times r}$ be submodules. Then

\[
\bigcap_{i=1}^m N_i = \ker \bigl(
O^{1\times r} \rightarrow (O^{1\times r} / N_1) \oplus \cdots \oplus (O^{1\times r} / N_m),
\;\; e_i \mapsto ([e_i],\ldots,[e_i]) \bigr).
\]
\end{enumerate}
assumptions:
Let $M = O^{1 \times n}/O^{1\times m}P$ and let $P_1,\ldots,P_m$ be the 
rows of $P$.
Let $N_1, \ldots, N_m \subset O^{1\times r}$ be submodules.
conclusions:
\mathrm{Ann}_M^{O} (v) 
= \ker (O \stackrel{\cdot [v]}{\rightarrow} M)
= \mathrm{LeftSyz}(\ (v,P_1,\ldots,P_m)\ ) \cap O e_1.
nodes.statement_short: Annihilators and intersections of submodules are computed as kernels of module homomorphisms, hence via syzygies.
nodes.label: corBasics

nodes.name: Kernels on quotient modules and practical feasibility
nodes.statement:
For an $O$-module homomorphism 
$O^{1 \times s}/O^{1\times r}Q \!\stackrel{\psi'}{\rightarrow} \!
O^{1 \times n}/O^{1\times m}P$, its kernel is the image of 
$\ker \psi$ (as in Theorem~\ref{propBasics}) under the natural projection 
$O^{1 \times s} \rightarrow O^{1 \times s}/ O^{1\times r}Q$. 
A left Gr\"obner basis can be obtained by reducing a
left Gr\"obner basis of $\ker \psi + O^{1\times r}Q$ with a left 
Gr\"obner basis of $O^{1\times r}Q$, see \cite{LV05}.\\


Note that in practical computations, elimination of module components 
is usually not complicated. This stands in distinct contrast with the 
elimination of algebra variables, which is often very hard to achieve. 
The algorithms used in this article involve only the elimination of 
module components and thus are feasible in practice.\\


The algorithms we have discussed are implemented in computer algebra systems like e.g. \textsc{Singular::Plural} \cite{Plural} or {\sc Maple} \cite{CQR, CS}  with the package \textsc{OreModules}. More background on these algorithms can be found in e.g. \cite{Kr}, \cite{LV05}. \\

In particular, a set of generators of $\ker(\kappa_p)$ from the
previous section can be calculated explicitly.

By Proposition \ref{EliOfCom}(2) $\ker(\kappa_p)$ is obtained via the kernel of a module homomorphism, that is, by one Gr\"obner basis computation with respect to module monomial ordering eliminating components. The monomial part of this ordering can be chosen arbitrarily to be e.~g.~a fast one.
nodes.statement_short: Kernels of maps between finitely presented modules, elimination of module components only, implementations in Singular::Plural and OreModules; $\ker(\kappa_p)$ by one Gröbner basis.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement:
By the definition of $R$ and Remark \ref{ann},  it is clear that 
$\left\lbrace p \right\rbrace \subseteq \mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace p \right\rbrace }^V $.

It remains to show that $\mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace p \right\rbrace }$ is most powerful. 
Suppose there exists another behavior $\mathcal{B}'$ unfalsified by $p$. The behavior $\mathcal{B}'$ 
possesses a kernel representation 
$R' \in O^{r' \times m}$.
By the definition of $R$, there exists a matrix $X \in O^{r' \times r}$ such that $R'=XR$. 
But since $(X \cdot R) \bullet p = X \bullet (R \bullet p)$, it follows that 
$\mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace p \right\rbrace }^V \subseteq \mathcal{B}'$.

possesses a kernel representation 
$R' \in O^{r' \times m}$.

But since $(X \cdot R) \bullet p = X \bullet (R \bullet p)$, it follows that 
$\mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace p \right\rbrace }^V \subseteq \mathcal{B}'$.

nodes.name: VMPUM of the cuspidal cubic over several Ore algebras
nodes.statement:
Let us consider a more interesting example than Example \ref{MotivatingExample}
with respect to our favorite algebras from Example \ref{interestingAlgebras}.  Let $\Omega=\{\omega\}$ 
consists of the cuspidal cubic $$\omega(t_1,t_2)=t_1^3-t_2^2.$$ 
Let us denote by $\mathcal{A}_O=\mathbb{C}[[t_1,t_2]]$ the ring of formal power series and consider the 
$\mathrm{VMPUM}$ $ \mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace \omega \right\rbrace }^V= \lbrace f \in
\mathcal{A}_O \; | \; R_{\mathrm{VMPUM}} \bullet f= 0 \rbrace $ of $\Omega$ with respect to several
operator algebras $O$.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item Suppose $O$ to be the second \textbf{Weyl algebra} (see Example \ref{interestingAlgebras}). Then
by using {\sc Singular} we obtain: 
$$ R_{\mathrm{VMPUM}} =  
\left[ \begin{array}{c} 
\partial_2^3 \\
\partial_1 \partial_2 \\
\partial_1^3 + 3 \partial_2^2 \\
t_2 \partial_2^2-\partial_2 \\
t_2 \partial_1^2 + 3 t_1 \partial_2\\
2 t_1 \partial_1+3 t_2 \partial_2-6
\end{array} \right]. $$ 
Now let us determine $\mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace \omega \right\rbrace }^V$ to see how 
precise the description given by the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ is. Let $f \in \mathcal{A}_O$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\partial_2^3 \bullet f = 0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; f=c_0 + c_1 t_2 + c_2 t_2^2, \;$ where
      $c_i \in \mathbb{C}[[t_1]]$.
      
\item $\partial_1 \partial_2 \bullet f = 0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; \partial_1\bullet c_1 + 2 t_2 \partial_1 \bullet c_2=0 
       \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; \partial_1\bullet c_1 =0  \; \wedge \; \partial_1\bullet c_2 =0$
      $  \Rightarrow \;\; c_1, c_2 \in \mathbb{C} $.
\item $ (\partial_1^3 + 3 \partial_2^2) \bullet f=0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; 
        \partial_1^3 \bullet c_0 +6 c_2=0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; 
        c_0 = -c_2 t_1^3 + d_2t_1^2 + d_1 t_1 +d_0, \;$ where $ d_i \in \mathbb{C}$.
\item $(t_2 \partial_2^2-\partial_2) \bullet f=0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; c_1=0 $.
\item $(3 t_1 \partial_2+t_2 \partial_1^2) \bullet f=0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\;
       d_2=0$. 
\item $(2 t_1 \partial_1+3 t_2 \partial_2-6) \bullet f = 0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\; 
       -4d_1t_1-6d_0 = 0 \;\; \Rightarrow \;\;d_1=0=d_0$.
\end{enumerate}
Hence, we obtain that $f=c(t_1^3 - t_2^2)$, thus 
$$ \mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace \omega \right\rbrace }^V= \{ c (t_1^3 - t_2^2) \ | \ c\in \mathbb{C} \}.$$
With respect to the requirement of being most powerful and linear, 
the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ is as significant as possible.
We observe that the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of a single non-zero 
signal has $\mathbb{C}$-dimension one. 
Actually, this holds in general, as will be shown in Theorem
\ref{CDimension}.
\item  Suppose $O$ to be the second \textbf{difference algebra} see Example \ref{interestingAlgebras}. Then
by using {\sc Singular} we obtain: 
$$R_{\mathrm{VMPUM}} = 
\left[ \begin{array}{c} \Delta_2^3\\
\Delta_1 \Delta_2\\
\Delta_1^3+3 \Delta_2^2\\
2 t_2 \Delta_2^2+\Delta_2^2-2 \Delta_2\\
2 t_2 \Delta_1^2+\Delta_1^2+6 t_1 \Delta_2+6 \Delta_2\\
8 \Delta_1^2 +21 \Delta_2^2 + 24 t_1 \Delta_1+36 t_2 \Delta_2-24 \Delta_1-18 \Delta_2-72
\end{array} \right]. $$ 
Similar arguments as above lead us to
$$\mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace \omega \right\rbrace }^V= \{ c (t_1^3 - t_2^2) \ | \ c\in \mathbb{C} \}.$$
\item Suppose $O$ to be the second \textbf{$\mathcal{SW}$ algebra} see Example \ref{interestingAlgebras}. Then
by using {\sc Singular} we obtain:
$$
R_{\mathrm{VMPUM}} = 
\left[ \begin{array}{c}
\Delta_2^3\\
\Delta_1\Delta_2\\
\Delta_1^3+3\Delta_2^2\\
2\partial_2+\Delta_2^2-2\Delta_2\\
2\partial_1+\Delta_1^2-2\Delta_1+2\Delta_2^2\\
2t_2\Delta_2^2+\Delta_2^2-2\Delta_2\\
2t_2\Delta_1^2+\Delta_1^2+6t_1\Delta_2+6\Delta_2\\
8\Delta_1^2+21\Delta_2^2+24t_1\Delta_1+36t_2\Delta_2-24\Delta_1-18\Delta_2-72
\end{array}\right]. $$
Note that generators in the output depend on the monomial ordering of the operators. 
In this example $\Delta_{1,2}$ were chosen to be greater 
that $\partial_{1,2}$. Taking a reverse ordering
produces different (but equivalent) answer.

Comparing this matrix with the matrix above, we see that the rows of the matrix belonging to
the difference case appear also here. We conclude that 
$$\mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace \omega \right\rbrace }^V= \{ c (t_1^3 - t_2^2) \ | \ c\in \mathbb{C} \}.$$
Thus, taking $\mathcal{SW}$ as operator algebra, we have got more equations 
than with the difference algebra. However, we have obtained very interesting mixed differential-difference equations, which show the interplay of two different operator settings.

 \item  The second \textbf{$q$-difference algebra} see Example \ref{interestingAlgebras}:
\begin{small} $$
R_{\mathrm{VMPUM}} = \left[ \begin{array}{c}
\partial_2^2+(-q^2+1) \partial_2\\
(-q-1) \partial_1+(-q^2-q-1) \partial_2+(q^4+q^3-q-1)\\
t_1^3 \partial_2-t_2^2 \partial_2+(q^2-1) t_2^2
\end{array}\right]. $$ \end{small}
\begin{enumerate}
\item The first equation yields:
\begin{align*}
&\;\; \sum_{i,j}c_{i,j}(q^j-1)^2t_1^it_2^j + (-q^2+1) \sum_{i,j}c_{i,j}(q^j-1)t_1^it_2^j = 0 \\
\Leftrightarrow & \;\;(q^j-1)^2+(-q^2+1)(q^j-1)=0 \\
\Leftrightarrow & \;\; j=0 \vee j=2.
\end{align*}
\item Now consider the second equation. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item Suppose $j=2$, then
\begin{align*}
& \;\;(-q-1)\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}(q^i-1)t_1^it_2^2  +(-q^2-q-1) \sum_{i,j}c_{ij}(q^2-1)t_1^it_2^2\\
& \;+(q^4+q^3-q-1)\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}t_1^it_2^2=0\\
\Leftrightarrow & \;\; (-q-1)(q^i-1)+(-q^2-q-1)(q^2-1)+(q^4+q^3-q-1)=0 \\
\Leftrightarrow & \;\; i=0.
\end{align*}
\item Suppose $j=0$, then
\begin{align*}
& \;\;(-q-1)\sum_{i,j}c_{i0}(q^i-1)t_1^i +(q^4+q^3-q-1)\sum_{i}c_{i0}t_1^i=0 \\
\Leftrightarrow & \;\; i=3.
\end{align*}
Thus \quad $f = c_{30} t_1^3 + c_{02}t_2^2$.
\end{enumerate}
\item Applying the last equation, we get 
\begin{align*}
\;\;t_1^3 c_{02}(q^2-1)t_2^2 -t_2^2 c_{02}(q^1-1)t_2^2 +(q^2-1) t_2^2 ( c_{30} t_1^3 + c_{02}t_2^2 ) =0\\
\Leftrightarrow \;\; t_1^3t_2^2(q^2-1)( c_{30} + c_{02} ) = 0 \;\; \Leftrightarrow \;\; c_{30} =-c_{02}.
\end{align*}
\end{enumerate}
Thus we obtain once more $\mathcal{B}_{\left\lbrace \omega \right\rbrace }^V= \{ c (t_1^3 -t_2^2) \ | \ c\in \mathbb{C} \}$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Computes with Singular the VMPUM of $t_1^3-t_2^2$ over the Weyl, difference, $\mathcal{SW}$ and $q$-difference algebras; always $\{c(t_1^3-t_2^2)\}$.
nodes.label: VMPUMex

nodes.name: Smaller generating sets of the VMPUM ideal
nodes.statement:
As we have seen in the previous example, 
the number of equations giving the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$
depends strongly on the underlying Ore algebra. 
In all cases, with Gr\"obner bases we get more equations than it might be actually necessary. 
However, it is possible to compute a smaller generating set, which is usually not a Gr\"obner basis.
Namely, one computes a left syzygy module of a given system and almost directly deduces 
a smaller generating set from it. As an example, we show that only 3 of 6 equations from the
first example of \ref{VMPUMex} generate the whole ideal,
namely $\partial_1 \partial_2, \partial_1^3+3 \partial_2^2, 2 t_1 \partial_1+ 3 t_2 \partial_2-6$. Analogous smaller generating sets
can be obtained for other examples.
nodes.statement_short: Gröbner bases give redundant equations; a syzygy computation yields smaller generating sets, e.g. 3 of the 6 Weyl equations suffice.

nodes.name: Kernel representation R of the VMPUM of several signals
nodes.statement:
A kernel representation of the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of 
$\Omega=\{\omega_1, \dots, \omega_N \}$ is determined by stacking a set of 
generators of $$\bigcap_{i=1}^N \ker( \kappa_{\omega_i} )$$
row-wise into a matrix $R$.

nodes.name: VMPUM of a finite signal set
nodes.statement:
Using the notation from above, the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $\Omega$ equals 
$$\mathcal{B}_{\Omega}^V= \left\lbrace g \in \mathcal{A}_O^m \; | \; R \bullet g=0 \right\rbrace.$$
conclusions:
the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $\Omega$ equals 
$$\mathcal{B}_{\Omega}^V= \left\lbrace g \in \mathcal{A}_O^m \; | \; R \bullet g=0 \right\rbrace.$$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.5
nodes.statement:
By the definition of $R$, it is clear 
that $\Omega \subseteq \mathcal{B}_\Omega^V$. Also the property 
of being most powerful follows by the same arguments 
as used in the proof of Theorem~\ref{vmpum}.
nodes.statement_short: Unfalsified by construction of $R$; most powerful by the argument of Theorem 4.2.

nodes.name: VMPUM of two signals over the first Weyl algebra
nodes.statement:
Suppose $O$ to be the first Weyl algebra and $\mathcal{A}_O=\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C})$.  
Consider the signal set $\Omega = \{ t, v_0 t-v_1 t^2\}$, 
where $v_0, v_1 \in \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}$. 
The second trajectory will appear in Example $\ref{wurf}$ again. Since
\begin{align*}
& \ker(\kappa_t) \cap \ker(\kappa_{v_0t-v_1t^2})\\  & = {}_{\mathrm{W}_1} \langle t \partial-1,\ \partial^2 \rangle  
\cap {}_{\mathrm{W}_1} \langle -v_0^2 \partial^2+(4v_1^2 t- 2v_0v_1)\partial-8v_1^2 ,\ \partial^3 \rangle \\
& = {}_{\mathrm{W}_1} \langle t^2 \partial^2 - 2 t \partial + 2 , \partial^3 \rangle, 
\end{align*}
the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $\Omega$ is given by
$ \mathcal{B}_\Omega^V=\{ c_1 t + c_2 t^2 \ | \ c_1, c_2 \in \mathbb{C} \}$.
The intersection of submodules of a free module 
over a Noetherian Ore algebra can be computed as in 
Corollary \ref{corBasics}, 
for instance with the system \textsc{Singular::Plural} \cite{Plural}.
nodes.statement_short: For $\Omega=\{t, v_0t-v_1t^2\}$ the intersection of kernels gives VMPUM $\{c_1t+c_2t^2\}$.

nodes.name: n-th Weyl algebra W_n
nodes.section: 5 VMPUM by using the polynomial Weyl algebra

nodes.name: Action of partial_i on polynomials
nodes.statement: Thus for $p \in\mathbb{C}[t_1, \dots, t_n]$, we obtain $ \partial_i \bullet p := \frac{\partial p}{\partial t_i}$.
nodes.section: 5 VMPUM by using the polynomial Weyl algebra

nodes.name: A_O is the space of smooth functions
nodes.statement:
Further suppose $\mathcal{A}_O $ to be $\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathbb{C})$, the space of 
smooth functions.
nodes.section: 5 VMPUM by using the polynomial Weyl algebra

nodes.name: VMPUM is finite-dimensional
nodes.statement:
A known result is that the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ is a finite-dimensional
vector space over~$\mathbb{C}$, since it is contained in the 
corresponding $\mathrm{MPUM}$ \cite{VMPUM}.
conclusions:
the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ is a finite-dimensional
vector space over~$\mathbb{C}$

nodes.name: Coefficients c_ik and exponents beta_ik
nodes.statement:
Suppose $p \in A^m$. Every polynomial $p_i$ can be written as 
$\sum_{k=1}^{h_i}c_{ik}t^{\beta_{ik}}$, 
where $c_{ik} \in \mathbb{C}$ for all $i,k$.

nodes.name: Exponent sets E_i and degrees d_ij
nodes.statement:
Let 
$\mathcal{E}_i:=\left\lbrace \beta_{i1}, \dots, 
\beta_{ih_i} \right\rbrace \subset \mathbb{N}_0^n$ denote the set of all 
exponent multi-indices occurring in $p_i$ and let
\begin{eqnarray} d_{ij}:=\max_{1\leq k \leq h_i} \left\lbrace (\beta_{ik})_j \; | \; \beta_{ik} \in 
\mathcal{E}_i \right\rbrace 
\end{eqnarray}
be the highest degree in $t_j$ of $p_i$.

nodes.name: Highest degree d_ij
nodes.statement:
d_{ij}:=\max_{1\leq k \leq h_i} \left\lbrace (\beta_{ik})_j \; | \; \beta_{ik} \in 
\mathcal{E}_i \right\rbrace
nodes.label: expo

nodes.name: Finite index set E_{p_i}
nodes.statement:
The set 
$$
\mathcal{E}_{p_i}=\{ \alpha \in {\mathbb{N}}_0^n \, | \, \alpha_j \leq d_{ij}+1 \; \mbox{ for } \, 1\leq j \leq n \}
$$
is finite, that is, $\mathcal{E}_{p_i} = \lbrace \alpha_{i1}, \dots, \alpha_{il_i} \rbrace$.

nodes.name: Derivative set Der_p
nodes.statement:
Define for $p\in A^m$
$$ \mathrm{Der}_p=\lbrace p_1, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{11}|}p_1}{\partial^{\alpha_{11}}}, 
\dots,\frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{1l_1}|}p_1}{\partial^{\alpha_{1l_1}}}, \, \dots \, , p_m, 
\frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{m1}|}p_m}{\partial^{\alpha_{m1}}}, \, \dots \,, 
\frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{ml_m}|}p_m}{\partial^{\alpha_{ml_m}}} \rbrace.$$

nodes.name: Polynomial syzygies Syz(Der_p)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)$ denote the module of polynomial syzygies.

nodes.name: Homomorphism Phi_p
nodes.statement:
Define for the matrix
$M=[ 1 e_1, \; \partial^{\alpha_{11}} e_1, \; \dots, \;
\partial^{\alpha_{1l_1}}e_1, \; \dots, \; 1 e_m, \; \partial^{\alpha_{m1}}e_m, \;
\dots, \; \partial^{\alpha_{ml_m}} e_m]^T$
the $A$-module homomorphism 















$$\Phi_p:\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p) \rightarrow \ker(\kappa_p), \;\;\; (q_1, \dots, q_l) \mapsto  (q_1, \dots, q_l) \cdot M, 
$$
which is clearly injective.
nodes.statement_short: $\Phi_p$ maps polynomial syzygies of $\mathrm{Der}_p$ into $\ker(\kappa_p)$ by multiplying with the operator matrix $M$; it is injective.

nodes.name: Image of Phi_p generates ker kappa_p
nodes.statement: ${}_{\mathrm{W}_n}\langle \mathrm{Im}(\Phi_p) \rangle = \ker(\kappa_p)$.
conclusions: ${}_{\mathrm{W}_n}\langle \mathrm{Im}(\Phi_p) \rangle = \ker(\kappa_p)$
nodes.statement_short: $\ker(\kappa_p)$ is generated by images of commutative polynomial syzygies of the derivatives of $p$.
nodes.label: KomCom

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement:
Evidently ${}_{\mathrm{W}_n} \langle \mathrm{Im}(\Phi_p) \rangle \subseteq \ker(\kappa_p)$. Now suppose that 
$a \in \ker(\kappa_p)$. Since every element in $\mathrm{W}_n$ can be written in 
normal form, 
we obtain
\begin{align*}
 a \bullet p & = \sum_k a_k \bullet p_k = \sum_k ( \sum_j c_{kj} t^{\beta_{kj}} \partial^{\gamma_{kj}} ) \bullet p_k \\
& = \sum_k ( \sum_j c_{kj} t^{\beta_{kj}})( \partial^{\gamma_{kj}} \bullet p_k ).
\end{align*}
Let us split the element $a$ in $a_z$ and $a_{nz}$ such that $a=a_z+a_{nz}$ and $(a_z)_k$ consists of the parts of $a_k$ where $\partial^{\gamma_{kj}} \bullet p_k$ is zero. 

By the choice of $d_{ij}$, the set
$\{ \partial_j^{(d_{ij} +1)} \, | \, 1\leq j \leq n, \; 1 \leq i \leq m \}$
generates the set of $\partial^\gamma$
with the property that there exists $1 \leq i \leq m$ such that 
$ \partial^\gamma \bullet p_i=0.$
Then $a_z$ is contained 
${}_{W_n}\langle \partial^{(d_{ij} +1)e_j} \, | \, 1\leq j \leq n, \; 1 \leq i \leq m \rangle$. 
But by the choice of $\mathrm{Der}_p$, the element $a_z$ is in the image of $\Phi_p$. 
Suppose $\partial^{\gamma_{kj}} \bullet p_k \neq 0$, then $\gamma_{kj}$ is equal or smaller than 
$(d_{k1}, \dots, d_{kn})$ in each component and again 
by the choice of $\mathrm{Der}_p$, the element $a_{nz}$ is contained in the image of $\Phi_p$. 
Thus it follows that $a \in \mathrm{Im}(\Phi_p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $a$ in normal form and split it into parts killing or not killing $p$; both lie in the image of $\Phi_p$ by the choice of $\mathrm{Der}_p$.

nodes.name: Easy inclusion
nodes.statement: Evidently ${}_{\mathrm{W}_n} \langle \mathrm{Im}(\Phi_p) \rangle \subseteq \ker(\kappa_p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Image of $\Phi_p$ lies in $\ker(\kappa_p)$.

nodes.name: Normal form expansion
nodes.statement:
Now suppose that 
$a \in \ker(\kappa_p)$. Since every element in $\mathrm{W}_n$ can be written in 
normal form, 
we obtain
\begin{align*}
 a \bullet p & = \sum_k a_k \bullet p_k = \sum_k ( \sum_j c_{kj} t^{\beta_{kj}} \partial^{\gamma_{kj}} ) \bullet p_k \\
& = \sum_k ( \sum_j c_{kj} t^{\beta_{kj}})( \partial^{\gamma_{kj}} \bullet p_k ).
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Take $a\in\ker(\kappa_p)$ in normal form and expand $a\bullet p$.

nodes.name: Split a
nodes.statement: Let us split the element $a$ in $a_z$ and $a_{nz}$ such that $a=a_z+a_{nz}$ and $(a_z)_k$ consists of the parts of $a_k$ where $\partial^{\gamma_{kj}} \bullet p_k$ is zero.
nodes.statement_short: Split $a=a_z+a_{nz}$.

nodes.name: a_z in the image
nodes.statement:
By the choice of $d_{ij}$, the set
$\{ \partial_j^{(d_{ij} +1)} \, | \, 1\leq j \leq n, \; 1 \leq i \leq m \}$
generates the set of $\partial^\gamma$
with the property that there exists $1 \leq i \leq m$ such that 
$ \partial^\gamma \bullet p_i=0.$
Then $a_z$ is contained 
${}_{W_n}\langle \partial^{(d_{ij} +1)e_j} \, | \, 1\leq j \leq n, \; 1 \leq i \leq m \rangle$. 
But by the choice of $\mathrm{Der}_p$, the element $a_z$ is in the image of $\Phi_p$.
nodes.statement_short: Annihilating monomials are generated by $\partial_j^{d_{ij}+1}$, so $a_z\in\mathrm{Im}\Phi_p$.

nodes.name: a_nz in the image
nodes.statement:
Suppose $\partial^{\gamma_{kj}} \bullet p_k \neq 0$, then $\gamma_{kj}$ is equal or smaller than 
$(d_{k1}, \dots, d_{kn})$ in each component and again 
by the choice of $\mathrm{Der}_p$, the element $a_{nz}$ is contained in the image of $\Phi_p$.
nodes.statement_short: Non-annihilating parts are bounded by the degrees, so $a_{nz}\in\mathrm{Im}\Phi_p$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus it follows that $a \in \mathrm{Im}(\Phi_p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $a\in\mathrm{Im}\Phi_p$.

nodes.name: VMPUM of a single non-zero signal is one-dimensional
nodes.statement: The $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $p \neq 0$ is a one-dimensional vector space over~$\mathbb{C}$.
also_stated_at:
We claim that the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of
a single non-zero signal has $\mathbb{C}$-dimension one.
conclusions: The $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $p \neq 0$ is a one-dimensional vector space over~$\mathbb{C}$.
nodes.label: CDimension

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.2
nodes.statement:
We use the notation of the Lemma \ref{KomCom}, which reduces to commutative calculations. It is easy to see that the equivalence  
\begin{align} s \bullet (f_1, \partial^{\alpha_{11}} \bullet f_1, \dots, f_m, \dots, \partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}} \bullet f_m)^T = 0 
\;\;\;\; \Leftrightarrow \;\;\;\; \Phi_p(s) \bullet f =0 
\end{align}
holds for every $ s \in \mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p) $. Now let us discuss the left hand side. More precisely, let us consider the solution space $\mathrm{Sol}(\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p))$ in $\mathcal{A}_O$ belonging to $\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)$. Since $\mathrm{Der}_p$ contains 
all non-zero derivatives of $p_i$ for all $i$, there exists a non-zero constant ${\mathbb{C}} \ni k \in \mathrm{Der}_p$. 
We can suppose $k=1$ and without loss of generality let 
$\partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}} \bullet p_m=1$. Then 
$$(-1, 0, \dots, 0, p_1), \; \dots, \;
(0, \dots, 0, -1, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{mh_m}|}p_m}{\partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}}}) \in \mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)$$
and thus 
\begin{align} \mathrm{Sol}(\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)) = \lbrace c \cdot (p_1, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{11}|}p_1}{\partial^{\alpha_{11}}}, \dots, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{mh_m}|}p_m}{\partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}}}) \; | \; c \in {\mathbb{C}} \rbrace.
\end{align}
Now suppose $f \in \mathrm{VMPUM}_p$. From Lemma \ref{KomCom} together with (\ref{SolDModCom}) and (\ref{SolCom}) we deduce the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via Lemma 5.1 to commutative syzygies of $\mathrm{Der}_p$; a constant in $\mathrm{Der}_p$ forces the solution space to be one-dimensional.

nodes.name: Reduce to commutative setting
nodes.statement: We use the notation of the Lemma \ref{KomCom}, which reduces to commutative calculations.
nodes.statement_short: Use Lemma 5.1 to reduce to commutative computations.

nodes.name: Equivalence of solution conditions
nodes.statement:
It is easy to see that the equivalence  
\begin{align} s \bullet (f_1, \partial^{\alpha_{11}} \bullet f_1, \dots, f_m, \dots, \partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}} \bullet f_m)^T = 0 
\;\;\;\; \Leftrightarrow \;\;\;\; \Phi_p(s) \bullet f =0 
\end{align}
holds for every $ s \in \mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p) $.
nodes.statement_short: Syzygy conditions on derivatives correspond to $\Phi_p(s)\bullet f=0$.

nodes.name: Consider the solution space
nodes.statement: Now let us discuss the left hand side. More precisely, let us consider the solution space $\mathrm{Sol}(\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p))$ in $\mathcal{A}_O$ belonging to $\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Consider the solution space of $\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)$.

nodes.name: A constant derivative
nodes.statement:
Since $\mathrm{Der}_p$ contains 
all non-zero derivatives of $p_i$ for all $i$, there exists a non-zero constant ${\mathbb{C}} \ni k \in \mathrm{Der}_p$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{Der}_p$ contains a non-zero constant.

nodes.name: Solution space is a line
nodes.statement:
We can suppose $k=1$ and without loss of generality let 
$\partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}} \bullet p_m=1$. Then 
$$(-1, 0, \dots, 0, p_1), \; \dots, \;
(0, \dots, 0, -1, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{mh_m}|}p_m}{\partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}}}) \in \mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)$$
and thus 
\begin{align} \mathrm{Sol}(\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)) = \lbrace c \cdot (p_1, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{11}|}p_1}{\partial^{\alpha_{11}}}, \dots, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{mh_m}|}p_m}{\partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}}}) \; | \; c \in {\mathbb{C}} \rbrace.
\end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Normalize the constant to 1; explicit syzygies force solutions to be multiples of the derivative vector.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Now suppose $f \in \mathrm{VMPUM}_p$. From Lemma \ref{KomCom} together with (\ref{SolDModCom}) and (\ref{SolCom}) we deduce the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemma 5.1 with (4) and (5).

nodes.name: Syzygy/solution equivalence
nodes.statement:
s \bullet (f_1, \partial^{\alpha_{11}} \bullet f_1, \dots, f_m, \dots, \partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}} \bullet f_m)^T = 0 
\;\;\;\; \Leftrightarrow \;\;\;\; \Phi_p(s) \bullet f =0
nodes.label: SolDModCom

nodes.name: Solution space of Syz(Der_p)
nodes.statement: \mathrm{Sol}(\mathrm{Syz}(\mathrm{Der}_p)) = \lbrace c \cdot (p_1, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{11}|}p_1}{\partial^{\alpha_{11}}}, \dots, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha_{mh_m}|}p_m}{\partial^{\alpha_{mh_m}}}) \; | \; c \in {\mathbb{C}} \rbrace.
nodes.label: SolCom

nodes.name: VMPUM is the most precise linear description
nodes.statement: In the case of a single non-zero signal, the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ gives the most precise description one can get for a linear system.

nodes.name: MPUM vs VMPUM of a thrown-ball trajectory
nodes.statement:
Consider the trajectory
$\omega(t)=v_0 t - v_1 t^2$, where $v_0,v_1\in{\mathbb{C}}\setminus\{0\}$.



Then the $\mathrm{MPUM}$ of $\omega$ is given by
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal{B}_{\{\omega\}} &= \{ \alpha (v_0t-v_1t^2)+\beta(v_0-2v_1t)+
\gamma (-2v_1) \ | \ \alpha, \beta, \gamma \in \mathbb{R}  \} \\
  & = \{ at^2 + bt +c \ | \ a, b, c \in \mathbb{R} \}\\
  & =  \{ w \in \mathcal{A}_O \ | \ \partial^3 \bullet w = 0 \}. 
\end{align*}
Thus there are three free parameters to choose. 
The $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $\omega$ is given by
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal{B}^V_{\{ \omega\}} & 
=\{ w \in \mathcal{A}_O \ | \  \left[ \begin{array}{c} -v_0^2 \partial^2+(4v_1^2 t- 2v_0v_1)\partial-8v_1^2  \\ \partial^3 \end{array} \right]  \bullet w = 0 \} \\
& = \{ c \, ( v_0 t - v_1 t^2 ) \ | \ c \in \mathbb{R} \},
\end{align*}
that is, two degrees of freedom vanish when we consider the time-variant model.
nodes.statement_short: For $\omega=v_0t-v_1t^2$ the MPUM is all quadratics (3 parameters) but the VMPUM is $\{c\,\omega\}$.
nodes.label: wurf

nodes.name: Degree in the Weyl algebra
nodes.statement:
Since every element of $\mathrm{W}_n$ can be transformed into normal form, 
the degree of an element $a\in\mathrm{W}_n$ can be introduced as
$$ \deg(a):= \max \lbrace \; \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i + \beta_i  \;\; | \;\; a = \sum_{\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{N}_0^n} a_{\alpha, \beta} 
t^{\alpha} \partial^{\beta}, \; a_{\alpha, \beta} \in \mathbb{C} \rbrace. $$

nodes.name: Degree filtration of W_n
nodes.statement:
Then $\mathcal{F}^i(\mathrm{W}_n):=\left\lbrace a \in \mathrm{W}_n \; | \; \deg(a)\leq i \right\rbrace $ induces a filtration 
on $\mathrm{W}_n$.

nodes.name: Associated graded ring of W_n is a polynomial ring
nodes.statement:
The 
corresponding associated graded ring $\mathrm{Gr}(\mathrm{W}_n)$ is isomorphic to 
$\mathbb{C}[t_1, \dots, t_n, \!\partial_1, \dots, \partial_n]$ as a graded $\mathbb{C}$-algebra.
conclusions:
The 
corresponding associated graded ring $\mathrm{Gr}(\mathrm{W}_n)$ is isomorphic to

nodes.statement: The dimension of $M$ is defined as $\dim_{\mathrm{W}_n}(M):=\deg(\mathrm{HP}_M)+1.$

nodes.name: Holonomic module
nodes.statement: Furthermore $M$ is called \textbf{holonomic} if it has dimension $n$.

nodes.statement:
A holonomic module is of 
minimal dimension, since the dimension of $\mathrm{W}_n$-modules is bounded below by $n$ and bounded

A holonomic module is of

conclusions: Holonomic $\mathrm{W}_n$-modules are additionally cyclic and torsion modules.

nodes.statement: As usual, we write $A=\mathbb{C}[t_1,\ldots,t_n]\subset \mathrm{W}_n$.

nodes.statement:
There is an isomorphism of $\mathrm{W}_n$-modules
$ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) \cong A.$
In particular, $\mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p)$ is simple holonomic $\mathrm{W}_n$-module.
conclusions:
There is an isomorphism of $\mathrm{W}_n$-modules
$ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) \cong A.$
$\mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p)$ is simple holonomic $\mathrm{W}_n$-module.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.5
nodes.statement:
Since $\kappa_p$ is a homomorphism of $\mathrm{W}_n$-modules, we get
$$ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) \cong \mathrm{Im}(\kappa_p) \subseteq \mathrm{W}_n / {}_{\mathrm{W}_n} \langle \partial_1, 
\dots, \partial_n \rangle \cong A. $$ 
Thus $ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) $ is isomorphic to a submodule of $A$. 
Due to the fact that $A$ is a simple holonomic $\mathrm{W}_n$-module and $ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) \neq 0$ 
the claim follows.
nodes.statement_short: Embed the quotient into $\mathrm{W}_n/\langle\partial\rangle\cong A$; since $A$ is simple holonomic and the quotient is non-zero, they coincide.

nodes.name: Embedding into A
nodes.statement:

$$ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) \cong \mathrm{Im}(\kappa_p) \subseteq \mathrm{W}_n / {}_{\mathrm{W}_n} \langle \partial_1, 
\dots, \partial_n \rangle \cong A. $$

nodes.statement: Thus $ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) $ is isomorphic to a submodule of $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence it is a submodule of $A$.

nodes.name: Simplicity concludes
nodes.statement:
Due to the fact that $A$ is a simple holonomic $\mathrm{W}_n$-module and $ \mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) \neq 0$ 
the claim follows.
nodes.statement_short: $A$ simple holonomic and quotient non-zero give the claim.

ideal $L_p$, depending on $p$, such that $\mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) $ 
is isomorphic to the cyclic left $\mathrm{W}_n$-module $\mathrm{W}_n / L_p $.

ideal $L_p$, depending on $p$, such that $\mathrm{W}_n^{1\times m} / \ker(\kappa_p) $

Suppose $\omega=[ c_1, \; c_2, \; c_3 ]^T$ for $c_1, c_2, c_3 \in \mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$. Then 
$$

Since
$$
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}

\right]
\cdot

\begin{eqnarray*}

nodes.name: Conversion of a polynomial to binomial representation
nodes.statement:
Let us describe how to find this representation. We restrict to the 
scalar and one-dimensional case, 
where $m=n=1$. The general case can be treated similarly. 
For $p \in A=K[t]$ we show how to find the introduced 
representation. Usually, a 
polynomial $p$ is given in the form 
$$p(x)=d_v t^v + d_{v-1} t^{v-1} + \dots + d_{1}t + d_0, \;\; \mbox{ where } d_i \in K.$$
To write $p$ in the form (\ref{darstellungvonp}), 
the occurring coefficients $c_{\nu}$ 
have to be determined. We will show how this can be done for a 
monomial $d_v t^v$. Since $\nu! p_{\nu} = t \cdot (t-1) \cdots (t-\nu+1)$, 
we define 
$$ g^{(\nu)}:=
t\cdot (t-1) \cdots (t-\nu+1) = t^{\nu} + g_{\nu-1}^{(\nu)} t^{\nu-1} + \cdots + g_1^{(\nu)}t.$$
First, the coefficients $g_{v}^{(\nu)}$ will be determined for $1 \leq v \leq \nu$ by 
using the fact that $g^{(\nu)}=g^{(\nu-1)} \cdot (t - \nu +1 )$.
\begin{enumerate} 
\item Determine $g_1^{(\nu)}$:\\
The polynomial $g^{(\nu)}$ is a multiple of $t$.
Recursively, one gets that 
$$g_1^{(\nu)} = 
\left\lbrace  \begin{array}{cc}
1 & \mbox{ for } \nu = 1\\
(-1)^{\nu - 1}  \prod_{k=1}^{\nu-1} k & \mbox{ for } \; \nu > 1. 
\end{array} \right.
$$  
\item Determine $g_2^{(\nu)}$:\\
Using $g^{(\nu)}= g^{(\nu-1)} \cdot (t\nu+1)$, we get
\begin{eqnarray*}
g_2^{(\nu)}& =& g_1^{(\nu-1)} - (\nu-1) \cdot g_2^{(\nu-1)} 
= (-1)^{\nu - 2} \prod_{k=1}^{\nu-2} k     \; - \, (\nu-1) g_2^{(\nu-1)}
\end{eqnarray*}
Since $g_2^{(2)}=1$, we get a recursive formula.
\item Determine $g_j^{(\nu)}$ for $j \leq \nu$:\\

A similar consideration as in the previous point yields
$$ g_j^{(\nu)}=g_{j-1}^{(\nu-1)} - (\nu-1) \cdot g_j^{(\nu-1)}.$$
\end{enumerate}
Finally, we observe 
\begin{eqnarray*}
d_v t^v &=& d_v \left(  g(v) -g_{v-1}^{(v)} \cdot g(v-1) - (g_{v-2}^{(v)}- 
g_{v-1}^{(v)}\cdot g_{v-2}^{(v-1)} )g(v-2) - \cdots \right)     \\
&=& d_v \left( g(v) + \sum_{i=1}^{v-1}k_v(i) \cdot g(v-i) \right)  
= d_v \left( v! p_v + \sum_{i=1}^{v-1}k_v(i) \cdot (v-i)! \cdot p_{v-i} \right) ,
\end{eqnarray*}
where
$$k_v(1):=-g_{v-1}^{(v)}, \;\; \mbox{ and } \;\; 
k_v(l)=\left\lbrace \begin{array}{ll} -g_{v-l}^{(v)}+\sum_{i=1}^{l-1}k_v(i) \cdot g_{v-l}^{(v-i)},  & \mbox{ if } l<v\\
                                       0, & \mbox{ if } l \geq v.
                                        
                 \end{array} \right. $$

nodes.name: ker kappa_p is finitely generated over S_n
nodes.statement:
Connecting remark \ref{BoundingIndex} and (\ref{shifttozero}) we get that $\delta^\mu p = 0$ 
for all $\mu$ with $\mu_i > \varrho_i $ for at least one $1 \leq i \leq n$. Now consider the finitely

$$ \mathrm{Shift}_p={}_{A}\langle \delta^\mu p \; | \; \mu \leq_{cw} \varrho   \rangle .$$
The corresponding syzygy module $\mathrm{Syz}( \mathrm{Shift}_p)$ is finitely generated too, 
since $A$ is a Noetherian ring. Analogously to the continuous case, 
we can give an 
$A$-module homomorphism from $\mathrm{Syz}( \mathrm{Shift}_p)$ to $\ker(\kappa_p)$, 
such that the image of $s_1, \dots, s_d$ under this map  
generates $\ker(\kappa_p)$, that is, $\ker(\kappa_p)$ is 
finitely generated as an $A$-module. 
This implies that $\ker(\kappa_p)$ is finitely generated as an
$\mathcal{S}_n$-module.

nodes.name: Discrete exponential function
nodes.statement:
For  $ \lambda = ( \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n ) \in K^n$ the discrete exponential function is given by
$$
 \exp_{\lambda}: \mathbb{N}_0^n \rightarrow K, \;\; t \mapsto \lambda^t= \lambda_1^{t_1} \cdots \lambda_n^{t_n}.
$$

nodes.name: WLOG nonzero exponential bases
nodes.statement:
Without loss of generality, we can assume 
$\lambda_i \neq 0 $ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$, since otherwise if $\lambda_j=0$
$$
p \exp_{\lambda} (t) = \left\lbrace 
\begin{array}{cc} 0 & \mbox{ if } t_j \neq 0 \\ g & \mbox{ if } t_j = 0 \end{array}, \;\; \mbox{ where }\right. 
$$
$$
g:\mathbb{N}^{n-1} \rightarrow K, \;\;\;\; t \mapsto  (p \exp_{\lambda}) ( t_1, \dots, t_{i-1}, 0, t_{i+1}, \dots, t_n).
$$

nodes.name: Automorphism chi_lambda
chi_lambda intertwines exponential shift
nodes.statement:
Since the equality
\begin{align*}
 \chi_{\lambda}(\Delta_i) \bullet (p \exp_\lambda) & = \frac{1}{\lambda_i}(\Delta_i - \lambda_i + 1) \bullet (p \exp_\lambda) \\

 &= \frac{1}{\lambda_i} \left( \lambda_i \exp_\lambda \sigma_i(p) - p \exp_\lambda  - \lambda_i p \exp_\lambda + p \exp_\lambda \right) \\
 & = \frac{1}{\lambda_i} \left( \lambda_i \exp_\lambda ( \sigma_i(p) - p ) \right) 
 = \exp_\lambda \Delta_i \bullet  p
\end{align*}
holds, we obtain the identity
$$  
\chi_{\lambda}(\Delta_i^k) \bullet (p \exp_\lambda) = \exp_\lambda \Delta_i^k \bullet  p
$$
that finally extends to
\begin{align} \chi_{\lambda}(\Delta^\mu) \bullet (p \exp_\lambda) = \chi_{\lambda}^\mu(\Delta) \bullet (p \exp_\lambda) = \exp_\lambda \Delta^\mu \bullet  p.
\end{align}
conclusions: \chi_{\lambda}(\Delta^\mu) \bullet (p \exp_\lambda) = \chi_{\lambda}^\mu(\Delta) \bullet (p \exp_\lambda) = \exp_\lambda \Delta^\mu \bullet  p.

nodes.name: Discrete shift equivalence, pairwise different exponents
nodes.statement:
Now consider 
\begin{align} p = \left[ \begin{array}{c} p_1 \exp_{\lambda^{(1)}} \\ 
\vdots \\ p_m \exp_{\lambda^{(m)}} \end{array}\right] , \;\; 
\mbox{ where } \;  \lambda^{(i)}  \in K^n \setminus \left\lbrace 0\right\rbrace,  \; \mbox{ and } \; p_i \in A
\end{align}
and suppose $\lambda^{(1)}, \dots, \lambda^{(m)}$ to be pairwise different and without loss of generality 
$\lambda^{(i)}_j \neq 0$ for all $1 \leq i \leq m$ and  $1\leq j\leq n$. Then 
\begin{align} \sum_{j=1}^m a_j \bullet (p_j \exp_{\lambda^{(j)}}) =0 \;\;\; \mbox{if and only if}\;\;\;[a_1, \dots, a_m] \in 
\bigoplus_{j=1}^m \chi_{\lambda^{(j)}}(\,\ker(\kappa_{p_j})  \,),
\end{align}
which follows by
$$\sum_{j=1}^m a_j \bullet (p_j \exp_{\lambda^{(j)}}) = 0 
\; \Leftrightarrow \; \sum_{j=1}^m \left(  \sum_{i=1}^{h_j} c_{ji} t^{\alpha_{ji}} \Delta^{\beta_{ji}} \bullet (p_j \exp_{\lambda^{(j)}})\right)  = 0 $$


$$\Leftrightarrow   \sum_{j=1}^m (\chi_{\lambda^{(j)}}^{-1}(a_j) \bullet p_j) \exp_{\lambda^{(j)}} =0 
\Leftrightarrow  \chi_{\lambda^{(j)}}^{-1}(a_j) \, \in \, \ker(\kappa_{p_j}) \;\; \mbox{ for all } \, 1 \leq j \leq m.$$
conclusions:
\sum_{j=1}^m a_j \bullet (p_j \exp_{\lambda^{(j)}}) =0 \;\;\; \mbox{if and only if}\;\;\;[a_1, \dots, a_m] \in 
\bigoplus_{j=1}^m \chi_{\lambda^{(j)}}(\,\ker(\kappa_{p_j})  \,),

nodes.name: VMPUM of discrete polynomial-exponential signals
nodes.statement:
Let $p$ be of the form (\ref{shiftexpvektor}). Further let 
$K_i:= \left\lbrace j \; | \; \lambda^j= \lambda^i \right\rbrace = 
\left\lbrace  k_{i1}, \dots, k_{i l_i}\right\rbrace $ and $l$ chosen minimal such that the disjoint union 
$K_1 \dot \cup \dots \dot \cup K_l = \left\lbrace k_{11}, \dots, k_{1h_1}, \dots, 
k_{l1}, \dots, k_{lh_l} \right\rbrace =\left\lbrace 1, \dots, m \right\rbrace $. Further define the vector 
$h_i:=[f_{k_{i1}}, \dots, f_{k_{il_i}}]^{T}$ and $H_i:=\chi_{\lambda^{(i)}}( \ker(\kappa_{h_i}) )$. 
Let  $e_{k_{ij}}$ denote the $k_{ij}$-th standard generator of $\mathcal{S}_n^{1 \times m}$ for 
$1\leq i \leq l$ and $1 \leq l \leq h_i$. Defining for $1 \leq i \leq l$
\begin{align*}
\phi_i: H_i \rightarrow \mathcal{S}_n , \;\;\; [a_1, \dots, a_{h_i}] \mapsto \sum_{j=1}^{h_i} a_j e_{k_{ij}} 
\end{align*}
the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $p$ is given by
$ \;\;\bigoplus_{i=1}^l \phi_i(H_i)$.
conclusions:
the $\mathrm{VMPUM}$ of $p$ is given by
$ \;\;\bigoplus_{i=1}^l \phi_i(H_i)$.

nodes.name: Dimension of the VMPUM of independent signals
nodes.statement:
Let $p=[p_1, \dots, p_m]$ consist of $\mathbb{C}$-linear independent signals.
We conjecture that $\dim_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathrm{VMPUM}(p))=m$.
conclusions: $\dim_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathrm{VMPUM}(p))=m$
